A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same BFtS research work. Text extraction and visual inspection covered all 24 pages of v4 and 27 pages of v5, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, without material reading gaps.

before.justification: Sections 3 and 5 and Appendix A report original synthetic and real-data experiments, benchmark comparisons, imputation results and ablations.

after.justification: V5 retains original empirical results and adds targeted-missingness comparisons, convergence diagnostics, large-graph evaluation and synthetic node-regression results.

M1.justification: BFtS retains its three players, classification and LDAM objectives, adversarial losses, handling of absent sensitive information, and alternating updates in Algorithm 1. Model and loss symbols are renamed. The regression experiment does not specify a revised BFtS training procedure.

E1.justification: V5 extends evaluation beyond binary node classification through synthetic fair node regression in Table 6. Figure 2 also adds a missingness scenario targeting particular label–sensitive-attribute combinations. The six real datasets remain; the larger synthetic classification graph scales existing coverage rather than introducing another domain.

E2.justification: Section 3 and Figure 2 add a targeted missingness heuristic as a comparator for the degree heuristic, alongside random missingness. The classifier and imputation baseline sets remain unchanged in corresponding experiments. The large-graph evaluation reuses existing baselines, and regression compares BFtS with the already-used Vanilla model.

E3.justification: V5 adds equalized-odds evaluation to the GCN and GAT comparisons and expands the observed-attribute sweep from 20–50% to 10–80%. New protocols include a 250,000-node, 100-feature synthetic graph and regression with group-specific Gaussian targets and MSE evaluation. Default observed-attribute fractions and existing labeled-sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V5 adds NBA training-loss convergence diagnostics, a large-graph scalability check and comparison of targeted versus degree-based missingness. Figure 8 expands sensitivity analysis over observed fractions but removes its simulation panel. The LDAM ablation, hyperparameter surfaces, representation visualization and BAIL worst-case trade-off analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both appendices state that results average ten runs and use the same existing practices of ± values and plotted error bars. V5 does not introduce additional seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests or a stated increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Previously reported table entries are retained, while v5 adds equalized-odds rows, targeted-missingness outcomes, expanded sensitivity curves, convergence curves and large-graph results. New large-graph training times are 85.4 minutes for BFtS and 114.6 for RNF. Regression Table 6 reports BFtS versus Vanilla MSE of 0.71 versus 0.65 and ΔDP of 0.15 versus 0.21. These are new evaluations, not performance improvements over v4 under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces AMMCB's minimized classifier fairness loss with AMAFC's explicit maximization of complete-data bias under nested training constraints. V5 adds a formal degree-bias assumption and a derivation involving true versus imputed demographic-parity gaps. It removes the minimum-k-union approximation discussion, corrects the final inequality in Theorem 2's proof and adds space complexity. The existing minimax theorems largely persist.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims: adversarial missingness can conceal bias, BFtS uses three-player worst-case imputation, and it improves the fairness–accuracy trade-off, including with no observed sensitive attributes. The revised conclusion summarizes these same contributions.

C2.justification: V5 adds a distributionally robust interpretation and explains why selective omission is plausible when data-integrity checks constrain tampering. V4's explicit privacy-misuse warning and Ethical Considerations discussion disappear. The worst-case fairness–utility trade-off, demographic-parity guarantee and lack of suitable large real-world datasets remain discussed.

D1.justification: V5 supplies setup information for the new experiments, including large-graph feature and group sizes, assortativity, regression target distributions and training times. Existing hardware, software, architecture defaults and code address remain unchanged. Regression-specific training and fairness-metric implementation details remain sparse.

R1.justification: V5 substantially expands positioning through work on adversarial omission in causal learning, manipulated data collection, distributionally robust optimization and degree-related vulnerability. Examples include Koyuncu et al., Fukuchi et al., Ben-Tal et al. and Subramonian et al. Existing references are largely retained; publication and citation-style updates do not constitute additional research changes.

P1.justification: The introduction, related-work passages, attack formulation and experimental overview undergo substantial rewriting. Model terminology is standardized, the preliminaries are consolidated, appendix discussions receive clearer subdivisions, and the worst-case trade-off and reproducibility discussions move. These changes extend beyond the citation-style and acceptance-header edits.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from four horizontally arranged heatmaps to six panels, Figure 8 is redrawn, and convergence and large-graph figures are added. Tables 3 and 4 gain metric rows and separate enlarged displays; regression receives a new table. V4's Figure 3 is retained as appendix Figure 10, alongside broader changes to plot styling and page layout.

improvement.justification: V5 clarifies the complete-data attack objective and adds useful scrutiny of the missingness heuristic, sensitivity and scalability, partially addressing v4's stated scale limitation. The overall gain is limited by sparse regression documentation, ambiguity in the new equalized-odds equation's stated averaging, and removal of the privacy and ethics discussion. The added validation nevertheless supports a modest net improvement.
